Dear Shalini Didi,

You asked on the phone why I sounded low lately. I thought it was just work stress. Deadlines, my manager, the usual. But by three every afternoon my shoulders felt like bricks, my head throbbed and I'd read the same email four times without it going in.
Then Imran at the next desk joked that I sit like a prawn. I laughed, but he was right. My laptop was flat on the desk and I was bent over it all day, hardly getting up.
So I tried small things. I put the laptop on a box, got a cheap keyboard, and started walking to the water cooler every time I finished a task. It sounds silly, but by the second week the afternoons felt clearer.
I'll still keep an eye on the headaches, and if they keep going I'll see the doctor.

Your brother,
Kamal

qa.a: He put the laptop on a box.

qa.a: Raising the laptop, using a separate keyboard and walking to the water cooler after each task eased his shoulders and cleared his thinking.

qa.q: How might Shalini have felt reading this letter?
qa.a: She was likely relieved that her brother had found what was dragging him down and was also planning to see a doctor if the headaches kept going.

grounding: It shows a professional who blamed stress for stiff shoulders, headaches and slow thinking, until small movement breaks and a better workspace lifted energy.

Pradeep, you've known Naveen the couch potato since college. So you want to know why I've started standing on calls? Fine, I'll tell you.
A month ago I was sure I was burning out. I'd come home from the office and just lie on the sofa, heavy and cranky. My neck was stiff all the time and I'd get these dull headaches after lunch. I told everyone it was stress.
Then one day the lift was broken and I had to walk up four floors to a meeting. I got there puffing, but weirdly, my head felt clearer than it had in weeks. That made me think.
So now I stand for calls, I take the stairs, and I raised my monitor with two old files. I'm not saying the stress vanished. But I'm less foggy, and the headaches are mostly gone. I still told my doctor about them, just to be sure.

qa.q: What did Naveen use to raise the monitor?
qa.a: Naveen raised the monitor with two old files.

qa.q: What made Naveen think again about blaming stress?
qa.a: After walking up four floors because the lift was broken, Naveen was surprised to feel clearer, and began to suspect that sitting still was part of the problem.

qa.q: What would you advise someone who feels like Naveen did?
qa.a: Try small movement breaks and a better screen height before assuming it is all stress, and mention ongoing headaches to a doctor.

qa.q: What would change for Pradeep if Pradeep noticed the same pattern at work?
qa.a: Pradeep might try standing on calls and taking the stairs too, instead of accepting a stiff, low afternoon as normal.

grounding: It shows a desk-bound professional who blamed stress for stiffness, headaches and sluggishness, and felt better after small movement breaks and a raised screen.

Manager's note, Thursday
Afreen, our data analyst, has mentioned headaches most afternoons this month and says it's just stress from the project. I've noticed a few other things. Her laptop sits flat on the desk, so she spends hours looking down. She eats lunch at her screen and rarely stands until six. By three she looks drained and her replies in meetings get short. Today I suggested we try two small changes: a laptop stand and separate keyboard, which the office has spare, and a ten-minute walking check-in with me at three instead of a desk meeting. Afreen was doubtful but agreed. After the walk she said her shoulders felt looser and her head clearer. We'll see how the week goes.
Irawati

Tuesday
Fourth headache this week. I told Reena it's the stress of the audit. She looked at me hunched over the laptop and said, 'Or maybe it's that you've been folded in half since nine.' She showed me a stretch where you clasp your hands behind your back and open your chest. My shoulders cracked. Embarrassing, but it felt amazing. So this afternoon I stacked two files under my laptop so the screen is higher, and set a reminder: every hour, walk to the water cooler and back. By five I was still tired, but the fog in my head had lifted, and no headache. I don't think the audit is the whole story. Small changes. Let's see if it holds.
Rukmini

passage:
At the cooperative bank in Tirur, Gopika sat at the same counter from ten to five, typing passbook entries with her shoulders creeping up towards her ears. By afternoon her head throbbed and her thoughts moved like jaggery in winter. "It's the stress," she told Usha, the cashier at the next counter.
"Or it's your chair," Usha said. "You haven't stood up since tea. And your screen is so low you're bowing to it."
Gopika laughed, but the next morning she put a thick ledger under the monitor and a cushion behind her back. Every hour, when the wall clock chimed, she walked to the water pot and back. By Friday the headaches were fewer and the afternoon slump had shrunk. Nothing else at the bank had changed.

qa.q: What did Gopika put under the monitor?
qa.a: A thick ledger.

qa.q: How does Gopika feel by the afternoon, and what does she blame at first?
qa.a: She feels drained and foggy with a throbbing head, and blames the stress alone.

qa.q: Which small changes lifted Gopika's energy?
qa.a: Raising the monitor, adding a cushion and walking to the water pot every hour.

qa.q: How does Usha see Gopika's afternoons?
qa.a: Usha notices that Gopika never stands and bows to a low screen, and suggests the chair is part of the problem.
